REU Site: Hands-On Undergraduate Research to Advancing Agricultural Robotics in the Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The overarching goal of this REU-site is to recruit and train talented undergraduates by immersing them in meaningful, hands-on research experiences that build technical expertise, enhance problem-solving skills, and prepare them for graduate studies and STEM careers. Central to this goal is engaging students in core robotics research areas—motion planning, sensor integration, control, localization, and human-robot interaction—while grounding these efforts in the specific needs and operational constraints of the RGV region. The program prioritizes the development of transferable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, and communication, recognizing that these outcomes are the most enduring benefits of research participation. While groundbreaking discoveries are welcomed, the program's true mission is to equip students with the knowledge, mindset, and abilities needed for advanced study and impactful STEM careers. The proposed REU-site seeks support for three annual summer cohorts of undergraduate students. Each year, ten students will join UTRGV for a ten-week immersive, research-focused experience in which the design and mock field-testing of robotic systems naturally immerse students in core robotics research topics while supporting broader exploration beyond the prototypes themselves. REU participants will work collaboratively in interdisciplinary teams and alongside UTRGV's graduate student population. Through this structure, the program aims to achieve the following objectives: Intellectual Focus: To conduct research in robotics aimed at advancing motion planning, sensor integration, control, and human-robot collaboration for systems intended to operate under the environmental conditions and operational constraints commonly found in rural and agricultural regions of the RGV. Educational Objective: To provide research opportunities for undergraduates—particularly those from the RGV, enabling them to contribute to solving regionally relevant engineering challenges while deepening their engagement through hands-on projects that connect directly to local agricultural and rural needs.

grant.title: Effect of Long-Term Inactivity on Railcar Bearing Lubricant Performance
grant.sponsor: University Transfportation Center for Railway Safety
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The performance of railroad bearings that sit idle in railyards, large industrial plants, or shipping ports has only recently been explored. Some of the bearings, with documented periods of inactivity exceeding 18 months, have been associated with major derailments. This provides a basis for concerns that the inactive periods contributed to early failure, possibly through degradation of the grease properties brought on by moisture intake or grease separation leading to uneven protection of the metal components. The proposed work builds on prior efforts conducted in collaboration with CSX Transportation and seeks to improve our understanding of the effects of long-term inactivity on lubricant properties. The proposed work would consist of (a) Preparation of test bearings which will be placed outdoors in a position to receive direct sunlight. (b) Placement of grease samples in the same location in a simulated bearing housing to mimic the thermal cycle of a sun-exposed bearing. (c) regular sampling from the simulated bearing housing to monitor long-term changes in lubricant performance and condition. (d) at intervals of 3 months, bearings will be removed and installed on a laboratory test rig and run for 1,000 simulated miles with continuous performance monitoring of temperature rise, vibration spectra, and power consumption, (e) post-test inspection including disassembly, teardown, and visual inspection of all bearing components, and (f) analysis of the grease composition at all stages with specific focus on loss of oxidation inhibitors and changes in tribological performance.

grant.abstract: This project investigates the role of IFIT3 and STAT1 genes in neuroinflammation associated with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). In humanized mouse models, the project will examine how HIV-1 infection alters IFIT3 and STAT1 expression and impacts the Jak/STAT signaling pathway in HAND. In mouse models, the project will characterize the contribution of these genes to amyloid-beta–induced neuroinflammation in AD. Finally, analyses of archived human brain tissues from HAND and AD patients will assess genomic and proteomic changes in IFIT3 and STAT1, providing insight into their regulatory roles in neuroinflammation and their combined contribution to HAND and AD pathologies.

grant.title: Open Educational Resources for Telecommunications and Networking
grant.sponsor: Texas Higher Education Coordinator Board (Sub-award through UT San Antonio)
grant.abstract: Cybersecurity is one of the most rapidly evolving multidisciplinary fields today. A 2022 study conducted by (ISC) 2 reports that the cybersecurity global workforce gap has grown to 3.4 million. More participants (43% to 48%) in the past year indicated that their organization lack proper time for assessment and oversight of processes, and that they experience slow patching of critical systems and inadequate time and resources for training as a consequence of staffing shortages. A key takeaway from the (ISC) 2 report is that from 2021 to 2022, practical skills and experience have become viewed as essential qualifications for those considering employment in the cybersecurity profession (in contrast to acquiring certifications alone). One challenge in providing these skills is that technology, both hardware and software, is constantly and rapidly evolving, and workforce training must stay abreast of the opportunities and ramifications surrounding these innovations. Although cybersecurity programs are proliferating in secondary and higher education, many do not have the resources to design, update, and deploy relevant and technical hands-on content in a collaborative environment. Our goal is to educate the next generation of cybersecurity students with the creative problem-solving skills and investigative mindset they need for today’s workforce. To address these industry challenges we propose an OER Implementation Program, entitled “ THECB Cybersecurity Foundations: Telecommunications and Networking ”.

grant.title: A Prototype Study of Distance Service Systems
grant.abstract: Distance service systems enabling remote delivery of traditional face-to-face services such as medical or psychological counseling, instructing, and dating have been an important societal aspect more than ever in this post-pandemic period. Many efforts have been attempted to optimize several critical sub-systems to build and run such distance service systems, including communication, data storage, and data analysis based on and for artificial intelligence (AI). However, little research seems to have been done to investigate how and whether those sub-systems can be integrated while maintaining their peak performances. In this project, we propose to implement a prototype distance service platform and use it to synthesize and evaluate existing techniques that optimize sub-systems to find out whether those techniques are still valid in an integrated environment. Based on our findings, we will then submit our recommendations regarding optimal tradeoffs among and limitations of those used techniques. Our project will initially focus on a prototype for a remote medical diagnostic system. The selection of medical diagnostic systems is simply that it is among the distance systems with the most stringent requirements on quality and most essential for society in case of another pandemic period. Our prototype will bridge several sub-systems: audio/video communication sub-system, an electronic medical record sub-system, and an AI data analysis sub-system. Upon successful implementation, we will scale it to a more general distance service platform. The delivery of our project will consist of a working and reusable prototype of the distance system and a report containing the information as outlined above. In addition, all our implementation will be open source and benefit society.

grant.abstract: Cybersecurity area, having the fastest job growth rate of 33% for 2020-2030 (BLS) and having demand index as high as 5 in some areas of Texas (Texas Workforce Development Toolkit), relies heavily on certifications to provide depth of knowledge. Out of 42,000 Texas vacancies, most are requesting certifications in CISSP, CISA, GIAC, CISM, and CompTIA+. The credential programs have been designed to provide both the breadth and depth of knowledge through stackable and convertible certifications while a student is pursuing BS in Cybersecurity(BSCS), MS in Informatics (MSIN), or earning certifications independent of the degree programs. The first five credential programs, consisting of three undergraduate certificates and two graduate certificates, provide breadth of knowledge in cybersecurity while a student stacks credits towards BSCS or MSIN degrees. The last three noncredit certification credentials provide depth in specific areas of cybersecurity while being convertible to technical electives for BSCS. The conversion mechanism allows one to change the underlying certifications per job market dynamics. These are also used for maintaining current certifications. The three undergraduate certificates divide the 52-SCH core of NICE-WFC compliant BSCS into three stackable short certificates (43-SCH), at the completion of which the remaining core consists of a capstone project and two technical electives. The two graduate certificates divide the 30-SCH MSIN into two stackable 12-SCH short certificates, at the completion of which a student may pursue 6-SCH of thesis or 6-SCH of designated electives to earn the master's degree. The designed accelerated credentials help in achieving 60x30TX goals.

grant.title: Center for Army HBCU/MI Research Centers of Excellence: Decentralized Ledger based Forensics Infrastructure
grant.abstract: 1 Motivation and ChallengesThe proposed research targets 1. Information Science, b. Research Area 2 DigitalForensics.Effective information collection, processing, and utilization play an increasingly important role ina variety of defense applications. As a result, the deployment of information systems becomesubiquitous. While the rich data that is unavailable in the past brings many benefits, it also createsnew challenges for forensics. For instance, it is hard to process the massive data to extractdigital evidence manually, and the complexity of the system brings a larger attack surface to theadversaries.The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) sheds light on the challenges and many successfulapplications have been developed. However, AI is a doubleedgedsword for digital forensics, i.e.,it has also been proved to be a powerful tool to generate fake evidence. Although new methods arealso proposed to combat AIgeneratedfake evidence, the situation is more like a catandmousegame. Furthermore, AIbasedforensics tools also suffer from all types of attacks such as datapoisoning and model poisoning, which can lead the tools to make wrong conclusions. Therefore,there is an urgent need to address these limitations to fully unleash the potential of AI in digitalforensics.2 The GoalThe goal of the decentralized ledger based forensics infrastructure is to protect the authenticity ofdigital evidence collected from different resources and offer the capability of tracing back whenan issue is detected. Instead of focusing on content analysis to detect/prevent malicious digital evidence,the team plans to adopt a different strategy to address the challenge of preserving the authenticityof digital evidence. Specifically, the team will design and develop a forensics infrastructurethat can provide a complete history of the lifecycle of digital evidence and offer the capability totrace back. From the original data collection to intermediate processing results and the final digitalevidence used for decision making, each step is authenticated and recorded in the system. Toachieve this goal, the proposed system should provide the following features: (i) Irreversible evidencerecording. When a record of digital evidence is added to the system, it cannot be removedor modified. (ii) Scalability. Considering the large number of data sources, the system must bescalable to handle all of them in an efficient manner. (iii) Flexible data authentication. Whilearbitrary data manipulation should be prevented, there are also legitimate operations that can be appliedto collected digital evidence (e.g., figure enhancement). Therefore, the system should allowthese operations without compromising the data authentication protection mechanism. (iv) Highresilience. The system will be deployed in a complex and hostile environment so it needs to beresilient against adaptive adversaries, and offer functionalities such as critical information leakagedetection and fault tolerance. (v) Privacy preserving auditing. A third party may occasionally needto check the correctness of digital evidence records managed by the system, but it does not need toknow the contents of the evidence.

grant.title: Establishment of an NSF I-Corps Site at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: This project at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) Center for Innovation and Commercialization (CIC) creates an NSF I-Corps Site. NSF Innovation Corps (I-Corps) Sites are NSF-funded entities established at universities whose purpose is to nurture and support multiple, local teams to transition their technology concepts into the marketplace. Sites provide infrastructure, advice, resources, networking opportunities, training and modest funding to enable groups to transition their work into the marketplace or into becoming I-Corps Team applicants. I-Corps Sites also strengthen innovation locally and regionally and contribute to the National Innovation Network of mentors, researchers, entrepreneurs and investors. The UTRGV-CIC is a center within the UTRGV Vackar College of Business and Entrepreneurship (VCOBE). The UTRGV- CIC was developed in order to accelerate the commercialization of student, faculty and regional innovations into the marketplace, foster and facilitate the exchange of ideas between the university and industry and prepare students to become entrepreneurs. This I-Corps Sites project: 1. Supports and expands an entrepreneurial culture in a region where entrepreneurs historically have not had significant assistance; 2. Expands opportunities for undergraduate and graduate business and STEM students so that they are able obtain hands-on experience in the implementation of product validation activities and to engage in real-world STEM-related business projects; 3. Assists STEM faculty to become more comfortable with the practice of marketing their inventions by introducing them to the I-Corps theory and practice of the I-Corps methodology; 4. Integrates the I-Corps methodology throughout the UTRGV infrastructure so that the university will be able to carry out its mission of "transforming Texas and the nation through the commercialization of university discoveries". There are several advantages to having an I-Corps site at UTRGV: being located directly on the U-S.-Mexican border, the UTRGV I-Corps is unique in that it the site is both binational and bicultural; and, the region that UTRGV serves is one of the fastest growing yet impoverished areas in the country. Promoting support for entrepreneurship in such a region demonstrates how well the I-Corps methodology works in a historically underserved area of the country. This project advances the commercialization of ideas that come from the STEM colleges and departments within UTRGV by providing STEM faculty and students with a methodology to promote their products and ideas in the marketplace. It also broadens the participation of normally underrepresented Hispanic students in the commercialization process. Ultimately, it will benefit the regional economy of deep-south Texas by providing support for start-up businesses and it will enhance the research enterprise at UTRGV through the creation of interdisciplinary teams.

grant.title: Collaborative Research: Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM, an Interdisciplinary Approach to Enhance Student Writing in STEM
grant.abstract: Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM (WATTS), an Interdisciplinary Approach for the Enhancement of Student Writing in STEM fields PROJECT DESCRIPTION Overview and Knowledge Base Undergraduate STEM writing skills, especially in engineering fields, need improvement1. Research has shown that students in STEM fields lack strong writing skills2. Although STEM students learn writing skills in first-year composition (FYC) courses, they often fail to transfer them to discipline-specific writing, mainly due to a perception that English courses are subjective and unrelated to their majors3. However, they view their major courses as fact-based and objective4,5. Therefore, writing skills that should continue to be developed throughout their undergraduate disciplines may remain stagnant.Despite the importance of discipline-specific writing skills, many instructors remain resistant to incorporating writing into their courses6. Engineering instructors report this resistance primarily due to large enrollments, lack of time, or poor quality of student writing7. In a recent study of engineering instructors, 60% perceived teaching assistants (graduate or undergraduate) trained to support writing to be the most valuable in helping them to include more writing in their courses7.Institutional efforts in STEM programs are often focused on retention, which justifiably impacts the approach to curricula, instruction, and funding for research efforts on and implementation of student interventions. In addition, given the cost of higher education, public pressure on institutions to graduate students within four years has increased, leading to programs that are intensive in the development of disciplinary competencies, with writing skills unintentionally becoming a secondary concern.To address these challenges, this application proposes to expand the implementation of the innovative and cost-effect Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM (WATTS) process which is focused on training generalist tutors to help students write better in the students’ own disciplinary genre. It also proposes to systematically evaluate its impact on outcomes related to students (and student writing), peer tutors, engineering instructors, writing centers, and writing tutor supervisors. While the current project research is being conducted in both engineering and engineering technology courses, the future goal is to expand it to other STEM fields. WATTS is founded on knowledge transfer theory and employs the frameworks of writing in the discipline (WID) and genre theory8,9,3. The collaborations between engineering instructors and writing centers enable instructors to provide WID support in their courses without adding substantially to their workloads; WATTS also has the potential to mitigate student misconceptions about writing and potentially produce better short- and long-term writing skill outcomes. The requirement to communicate with peers outside of engineering provides students with a learning opportunity that extends past basic writing skills and promotes WID10. The results of our preliminary research on WATTS have motivated the formulation of this proposal’s Specific Aims:Specific Aim 1: Determine the impact of WATTS on student- and tutor-level outcomes. Identify mitigating and moderating effects of WATTS using data from students and tutors.• Objective 1.1: Identify the effects of WATTS on student perceptions and likelihood to use tutoring.• Objective 1.2: Identify the effects of WATTS on student writing.• Objective 1.3: Identify the effects of WATTS on tutors’ self-efficacy and tutoring practices.Specific Aim 2: Determine the impact of WATTS on instructors and on writing center outcomes to enhance the implementation, training, and development of WATTS.• Objective 2.1: Identify instructor attributes that contribute to successful WATTS implementation.• Objective 2.2: Identify writing center attributes that contribute to successful WATTS implementation.• Objective 2.3: Identify elements of joint training of instructor and tutor supervisor that contribute to WATTS successful implementation.

grant.abstract: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) located in the border region of United States and Mexico is seeking to increase participation, retention and graduation rates among minority low-income students in the critically needed engineering and technology programs. This project provides innovative ways for adapting effective evidence based curricular and co-curricular activities aimed to improve undergraduate student academic success. The primary goal of this project is to encourage and increase the number of students towards obtaining their degrees in STEM by providing 30 undergradaute students with four-year scholarships, and 17 undergraduate students with two-year scholarships (47 total), spread across four cohorts. In addition, we emphasize on improved student technical workforce readiness levels by establishing an academic support system at the College of Engineering and Computer Science (COECS) to encourage students to pursue careers in emerging fields of engineering and technology. Building on existing student support services at UTRGV, this project includes technical and academic success workshops, professional development, peer mentoring, industry certifications and internships, and developing course modules integrated with Engineering Technology and Manufacturing Engineering curriculum. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (a) To increase student enrollment of Manufacturing and Engineering Technology undergraduate programs created to train and prepare students with high-tech skills in the fields of manufacturing, automation and systems engineering; (b) Developing an Eco-System in COECS with tailored student centric activities to address student’s precollege experience, social-cultural experience, institutional experience, and college experience specifically targeting underrepresented demographics; (c) Financially support undergraduate students by awarding S-STEM scholarships over the grant period; and (d) Build partnerships with industry to provide more learning and internship opportunities for students.

grant.title: Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger
grant.abstract: Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger PI: Hansheng Lei Co-PI: Xu Lei, Liyu Zhang, Fitra Khan, Mahmoud Quweider Motivation and challenges. The Internet of Things (IoT) aims at to build an architecture to integrate a wide variety of devices for computation, sensing, communication, and actuation. This concept is then extended to the Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) that can connect all types of units in the battlefield to enable predictive analytics for intelligent command and control and battlefield services. Considering the complexity of IoBT deployment environment, an edge-cloud architecture is a suitable way to connect IoBT devices. Edge computing datacenters are deployed closer to the physical places where IoBT devices are used, and this allows data to be collected and processed locally. IoBT applications running in different edge computing datacenters only need to interact with each other through the cloud datacenter when necessary. Therefore, this architecture greatly reduces unnecessary communication and latency. Furthermore, the edge-cloud paradigm is also consistent with the design of 5G network, which is believed to be critical for DoD. Systems built on top of an IoBT infrastructure, especially systems involving AI, rely on data collected by IoBT for making support decisions and conducting operations of critical infrastructure. A failure of preserving the integrity of such a system can cause serious consequences. However, there is a lack of end-to-end protection of IoBT and systems built on top of it, especially AI systems, which prevents fully unleashing the potential of IoBT. The goal. The goal of the proposed efforts is to provide end-to-end protection of key IoBT applications, which is achieved through the following objectives: (i) A novel blockchain architecture that is designed to work with IoBT and able to handle a large number of IoT devices in an efficient manner; (ii) an end-to-end IoBT infrastructure protection mechanism based on the newly proposed blockchain architecture, especially for AI systems built on top of it; and (iii) a prototype implementation of the proposed framework and a testbed environment for benchmarking. Technical approach. The proposed blockchain based end-to-end IoBT protection solution consists of two major components: (i) A novel blockchain scheme that is integrated with edge-cloud architecture and able to support a large number of IoBT devices; and (ii) an integration of the protection mechanism into the proposed blockchain scheme to guarantee the effectiveness of IoBT applications running in the edge-cloud environment. The novel blockchain scheme consists of multiple edge-blockchains and one cloud-blockchain, where multiple edge-blockchains can support massive number of IoBT devices, and the new protocols proposed herein allow each of the blockchains to verify information stored on other blockchains in an efficient way. This novel blockchain scheme is then leveraged to protect AI systems through two steps: protecting the data collection procedure and protecting the model building procedure, which is usually expensive and hard to verify. Due to the immutability feature of blockchain and our novel stochastic checking mechanism, an adversary cannot compromise the integrity of an AI system without tampering with the majority of the peers of the proposed blockchain system. Expected results. The expected results of the proposed efforts are three-fold: (i) The design and implementation of the edge-cloud blockchain and integrated protection mechanism for IoBT applications, especially AI related applications; (ii) a testbed to benchmark the developed system and future systems such as distributed asynchronous processing and analysis of things; and (iii) involving undergraduate and graduate students in research and development in IoT and IoBT areas.

grant.title: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
grant.abstract: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. Specifically, an ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification (HDH) desalination process will be demonstrated in a lab scale. Innovative approaches include: (i) a floating system directly situated in the coastal water with no seawater intake and no brine discharge, (ii) a fully nature-powered mechanism directly driven by multiple renewable energy sources with zero usage of electricity, and (iii) a unique humidifier design using cloth wetting and wave overtopping to enhance mass transfer. The enabled desalination plant will be simple, robust, and environmentally-friendly, and is expected to produce freshwater in both large and small scales cost-effectively to meet diverse needs. Water quality analysis will be conducted in parallel with the technological advancement. The requested funds will be used to cover expenses on: wages for three graduate research assistants, summer salaries for three faculty members (the applicants), materials and supplies for the lab-scale prototype construction and water quality analysis, small instruments for testing the prototype, travel fees, and indirect costs. The proposed project will contribute to accomplishing the objectives 1, 2, 4, 5 defined in Water Desalination Act of 1996 as amended by WIIN Act and the objective 5 defined in Desalination 2008 , as listed in page 2 of the FOA.

grant.title: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant Introductory Sequence to Build Computational Skills
grant.abstract: Computational knowledge and skills have become essential to all disciplines and economic sectors. The ubiquity of computing impacts how we educate and prepare the future workforce regardless of one’s chosen career pathway. Thus, it is imperative to develop non-CS undergraduate students’ essential skills in solving problems computationally in their discipline and in possessing knowledge of ethical concerns related to growing cyber threats and vulnerabilities. To address this need, three institutions of higher education are collaborating as a Networked Improvement Community [NIC]: The University of Texas at El Paso [UTEP], Texas A&M University Corpus Christi, and the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. The aim of improvement at each institution is to raise non-CS students’ motivation to pursue knowledge of computational skills and become aware of ethical and security issues. The proposed project has three objectives to meet its goal of developing non-CS students’ skills for solving problems using computation: (1) develop and refine outcome-focused, problem-based, discipline-relevant course modules for creating course sequences that are adaptable to varying institutional context and disciplinary degree programs; and (2) incorporate inclusive practices into delivery of the modules to retain and advance students in the computational sequence. Intellectual Merit. UTEP is the lead institution and Alliance Backbone of the NSF-funded National CAHSI (Computing Alliance for Hispanic-Serving Institutions) INCLUDES Alliance. The Alliance aims to broaden participation of Hispanics in computing using the conditions of collective impact, an improvement science framework closely aligned with NICs. With its 12-year history of building and supporting academic partnerships, CAHSI and its Backbone team are well positioned to support the IHE partnership in the proposed work, which aligns with CAHSI’s mission of growing and sustaining a networked community focused on advancement of Hispanics in computing. The proposed project has defined a collection of modules focused on problem-solving, computational thinking, cybersecurity, and ethics that can be used to create a sequence for STEM, non-CS majors that is adaptable to local context. In addition, the Alliance Backbone will support the professional development of instructors involved in the project with evidence- and research-based inclusive practices, which are especially important for success of Hispanics and other individuals from underrepresented groups. Using the improvement science framework with feedback from the external evaluator, the investigators and STEM subject matter experts from the partner institutions will critically review and iteratively improve organizational structures, course modules, and sequences. The investigators have expertise in working with interdisciplinary projects and are committed to collaborate in refinement of a reconfigurable, introductory course sequence designed to prepare the future STEM workforce with computational knowledge and skills. Broader Impacts. The partner institutions are Hispanic-Serving Institutions [HSIs] with majority Hispanic populations. Working with non-CS departments, the project will serve a significant number of women who are over-represented in the partnerships’ STEM fields (other than Physics) involved in the project. This has potential to broaden participation of students from underrepresented groups in computing, a priority of the NSF. The proposed modules are adaptable across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Because the Alliance operates as a network of networks, it has numerous outlets for disseminating modules to both Alliance institutions and other HSIs. One such outlet is the Alliance’s non-profit-organization partners, Excelencia in Education and Great Minds in STEM, that are national Hispanic organizations sharing a core purpose of increasing the number of Hispanics who are competitive in higher education generally and in computing specifically.

grant.title: Computational Studies of Snake Venom
grant.abstract: Snake venoms are complex mixtures of toxins. Most major venom toxins have been characterized and their transcripts have been identified from many different snake species. However, the toxin-toxin interactions in the venom remain poorly understood. Therefore, the goal of this proposed project is to decipher the venom complexity by using Crotalus atrox venom as a model system. We will integrate biochemistry and computational approaches to detect the toxin-toxin interactions and simulate the three-dimensional structures of toxin interactions. The expected results will advance our knowledge about how venom toxins assemble into venom complex units to synergistically strengthen their toxic activity.

grant.title: Synthesis of Engineered Cementitious Composites (ECC) for Applications in Texas
grant.abstract: Among the groups of High-Performance Fiber-Reinforced Cementitious Composites (HPFRCC), Engineered Cementitious Composites (ECC) is a special type that is characterized by high-ductility (3-5% of strain) and moderate tensile strength (4-6 MPa) with 1.5-2% fiber contents by volume. Under tensile deformation, ECC shows a strain-hardening behavior and closely spaced microcracks after the first cracking. ECC has excellent shear capacity, improved damage tolerance, ability to control crack width, and synergistic interaction with reinforcing bars. The initial cost of ECC is higher than the regular concrete, but the use of ECC may reduce the life-cycle cost and corresponding environmental impact and provide improved safety because of the superior ductility. The objective of this project is to identify the applications in which the use of ECC can be applicable in Texas transportation system. To achieve this goal, the performing agency shall conduct seven tasks categorized into three activities: (1) a comprehensive literature review with in-depth meta-analyses, (2) a survey for state, federal, and international agencies, and (3) a cost-benefit analysis considering Texas environment, life-cycle cost, and environmental impact. Based on the collected data and analysis, the recommendations on ECC applications in Texas and considerations in mixture-design, production, and constructions of ECC shall be provided.

grant.title: TRUSTVILLE: Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment
grant.abstract: Getting students’ interest piqued in a college degree in a STEM field is challenging. However, due to ever increasing pace of technology transformation, the area of computer science is frequently afforded an opportunity to attract students to relatively new areas with visible impact on everyday life and business. Cyber security, a field pervasively touching almost every aspect of modern life, boasts a promise of job growth of 28% from 2016 through 2026 according to BLS. On the other hand, according to ISACA, 84% of organizations believe that only half or fewer of the applicants for security jobs are qualified. This proposal is for enhancing Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on a Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment (TRUSTVILLE). The proposed integrated security lab, which includes Internet of Things (IOT) equipment as well, will be familiarizing students with the state of the art cyber security appliances and software in a realistic environment to give them a competitive edge in the job market for serving to fill the existing gap in cyber security in public and private sectors. The Computer Science Department at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has been offering courses in cyber security area, however, a formal cyber security track with the required training has not been offered due to lack of hardware and software. The institution has Data, Intelligence and Security (DIS) group, with its own lab space, and prides itself for hosting the first International Conference on Data, Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) in April 2018. Given the current faculty expertise in cyber security, experience in teaching related courses, having a DIS group with its own lab space and the market potential for cyber security jobs, the university is strategically poised for offering a specialized track in cyber security to enhance teaching and research. Due to the market demand, the hardware and software related with cyber security are expensive, and this proposal is for securing funds to assist the institution’s ongoing efforts to establish a market driven cyber security track supported by a modern cyber security integrated laboratory. Since low traffic volume is encountered in a lab environment, expensive high-performance ASIC based hardware is not needed. However, the updates to the firmware and software of security hardware, and to the software itself could be as frequent as daily, for example, to block vulnerabilities including zero-day worms. Therefore, most of the expense of cyber security integrated lab is not in the hardware, but rather in the annual subscription of the software to keep the lab current. The cyber security track in computer science will consist of seven computer science courses geared towards cyber security, three criminal justice courses, and a senior cornerstone project in the area of cyber security. All of these courses will incorporate Project Based Learning (PBL) methodology to familiarize the students with industry grade cyber security tools and appliances. The required integrated laboratory will consist of a gamut of cyber security related hardware and software to understand and analyze the weaknesses of systems and procedures and learn how to strengthen security at different levels. The integrated security laboratory will consist of software and hardware such as IoT devices, IPS, IDS, threat hunting, vulnerability management, traffic monitoring, penetration testing, forensics, encryption, network security and endpoint security for both on premise and cloud assets.

Prototyping and Testing of Electrically Conductive Thermoplastic Poyurethane Railroad Suspension Pad
grant.sponsor: University Transportation Center for Railroad Safety
grant.abstract: This research will take formulations of carbon nanofibers in thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPU), which have shown promising levels of electric conductivity, for use in a conductive steering pad, and prepare them for deployment in a commercially viable product. Plain elastomers are insulators and prevent transmission of current from rail to frame to signal door or gate opening devices. In addition, the thermal insulating properties of these materials reduce the rate of heat flow from bearings through the bearing adapter and into the side-frame, where it can be dissipated. Previous studies performed by the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) revealed that traditional conductive additives, such as carbon black, must be applied at high volume fraction in order to generate sufficient conductivity, which in turn results in substantial increases in pad stiffness and degradation of pad durability. Vapor Grown Carbon Nanofibers (VGCNF) are extremely efficient conductive additives that can produce the desired conductivity at much lower concentrations and with less impact on mechanical performance than traditional additives. Prior efforts have identified a TPU carbon nanofiber combination and fiber loading that produces excellent conductivity, and results in an electrically conductive part when molded under commercially useful molding temperatures. The identified system first needs to be scaled from laboratory quantity testing to injection molding quantities, and then prototyped. Moreover, the microstructural contributions to conductivity as well as the allowable processing range need to be fully described in order to support process development and quality control processes in commercialization.

grant.title: IBSS-L: The Effect of Co-Designed Accessible STREAMS Apps on Inclusion of Hispanic Pre-school Students with Disabilities
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The purpose of this interdisciplinary research study is two-fold. First, it is to investigate if pre-school general and special educators’ collaborative experience in designing and implementing cloud-based STREAMS (science, technology, reading, engineering, arts, mathematics and self-regulation) curricular applications (Apps) for their students with disabilities influences their attitudes toward inclusion, their collaborative behaviors, and their attitudes toward their own teaching effectiveness. Second, it is to explore the effect of accessible technology-based STREAMS Apps on learning outcomes of pre-school students with disabilities (SWDs) and the engagement of their parents. Engaging students in learning of STEM at an early age is critical for preparing these students for success in STEM careers as adults. This study addresses disparities due to ethnicity, socioeconomic status (SES), and disabilities. It is intended to garner the collaborative creative efforts and expertise of a multidisciplinary (social-behavioral-economic sciences and education) research team housed within the Special Education Research Consortium of College of Education, P-16 Integration, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. This study will facilitate Brownsville Independent School District in meeting their district improvement goals on pre-school inclusion. Based on needs survey findings, STREAMS research team proposes to use two-week teacher summer institutes and three to five parent support workshops for teachers and parents to design accessible pre-school curriculum for students with disabilities (SWDs) based on Universal Design for Learning theoretical framework. Knowing the value of engaging parents of SWDs, the research team will provide parent support workshop that are family-centered and child-focused. This 3 year project covers 16 iPads for SWDs, stipends for teacher training, incentives for parent participation, and one month pay for each team member and part-time staff assistance. Research Design: The STREAMS research team will use a mixed methodological approach to address the following research questions. 1.What are the effects of co-designing STREAMS on teachers’ attitudes toward the collaborative experience, inclusion, and changes in teachers’ self-efficacy? 2.What are the effects of STREAMS on SWDs’ learning outcomes? 3.What are the effects of STREAMS on parental engagement in their child’s education? The team will collect survey and interview data. In addition, the team will measure the pre-/post and one-year post differences on SWDs’ learning outcomes. This will be accomplished using curriculum-based measures and norm-referenced instruments that measure across domains of academic and social-emotional skills. Intellectual Merit : This study will contribute to STEM knowledge base in two ways. The produced curricular applications (apps) will increase pre-school children’s interest toward STEM fields and accelerate the social and cognitive learning of pre-school children with or without disabilities. Further, very limited research studies have been done using UDL framework and principles and, of the few, the application of this framework is in math, science, and engineering (Rose & Gravel, 2010). The team of general and special teachers will operationalize UDL framework to ensure that the end product is accessible to all learners, especially SWDs, in pre-school settings. Broader Impacts : This study can interrupt the cycle of academic failure and develop a new trajectory for Hispanic children with disabilities. Successful SWDs’ learning outcomes reduce social costs in welfare support and empower SWDs to lead productive and fulfilled adult life through accessible technology and inclusion. It will allow opportunities for teachers to collaboratively develop evidence-based pedagogical content knowledge in STEM and will capitalize on the cultural and linguistic capitals of young Hispanic SWDs through parental collaboration. This research project examines factors that maximize the potential of the child with disabilities for inclusion through collaborative teaming and technology use. It will provide schools with an evidence-based inclusion model for sustainable inclusion practice and strengthen collaborative partnership between local school district and UTRGV Special Education Research Consortiums. Most importantly, it will strengthen the moral and social foundations of U.S. education and advances U.S. in building STEM education in a socially just fashion.

grant.title: Fusing Ultrasound and Vision Processing for Assessing Indurations
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: Indurations, such as appearing as a result of PPD or tuberculin test, are assessed using finger feel method largely to measure the size of the swelling. For example, in case of PPD test, if the induration is 10mm or less, then the test is considered to be negative. In case of positive test, the patient needs to go through medication for about a year which in itself can cause side effects whereas the process may have been unnecessary. The proposed project is to build an inexpensive portable instrumentation to provide alternative to subjective testing of indurations, and provide more scientific approach to assessment of indurations. Indurations have two aspects in general. Firstly, the visual aspect such as the shape of the bump, color/hue, and the size. Secondly, an induration has the feel aspect such as the hardness. Both aspects need to be measured to provide more scientific assessment of an induration. The visual aspect of an induration will be measured through a stereo imaging system. The feel aspect of an induration will be measured through an ultrasound system. 3D signal processing will be performed on the data acquired from both systems to fuse both systems to produce scientific based assessment of an induration. The testing will be done on artificial arms with simulated indurations.

grant.abstract: Mobile computing, especially in the form of smart phones and tablets, is fast replacing the use of desktop computers and laptops. Faculty must take full advantage of this paradigm shift by introducing the new technologies into the curriculum and the classroom. This will provide students with a broader access and a deeper immersion into technology. Recent surveys have shown that most of the devices students have today are connected to the internet and can run apps capable of supporting graphics and multimedia. Faculty can judiciously integrate such devices into their instructional approach to deliver course content to students in an individualized manner; implement interactive and asynchronous activities; embed and collect assessment- and instruction-related data; and facilitate communication among students. The goal of this proposal is to create a BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) instructional model, including development of Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) course-specific apps; implement the model in key CIS courses; and study the impacts of model implementation on students. Key measures will include (anticipated) improvements in student accessibility, interest and engagement, retention, and course performance; and the model will undergo continuous evaluation and refinement. We aim to study the effects of introducing one-to-one results-driven learning and instruction, via personalized technology (BYOD and mobile apps), into the core CIS courses of Programming Fundamentals I and II (PF-I, PF-II), and Discrete Structures (DS), to determine whether the new model improves interactivity and engagement, as well as accessibility and time spent on course material. We will assess the behavior and learning of first- and second-year students to determine specific behavioral patterns, rates of learning concepts, and the extent to which embedded computer science concepts are learned. grant.title: Disjoint NP-pairs and Structural Properties of Complete Sets
grant.abstract: A (disjoint) NP-pair is a pair of disjoint, nonempty sets in the complexity class NP. The study of disjoint NP-pairs is motivated by their relations to public-key cryptosystems and to propositional proof systems. In particular, answers to questions about existence of NP-hard or P-inseparable NP-pairs informs us about the question of whether secure public-key cryptosystems exist; existence of complete NP-pairs is implied by existence of optimal propositional proof systems. This project will investigate P-inseparable and complete NP-pairs further, in particular whether they can be derived from a hypothesis that is weaker than any of the known ones, and whether existence of these NP-pairs have strong consequences that are unknown before. We will examine commonly (dis)believed hypotheses in complexity theory such as that NP≠coNP and that PH collapses, and research on their relations to the existence of P-inseparable and complete NP-pairs. It is also our goal to build on recent results regarding relations between NP-pairs and propositional proof systems and obtain deeper insight into both subjects. It is important to study structural properties of complete sets because they gives us a better understanding of the computational power of various complexity classes, and also might lead to proofs of separation results in complexity theory. The proposed project will focus on the following structural properties of complete sets: - Robustness: does a complete set remain complete if certain amount of elements are taken away from the set? - Autoreducibility: does a complete set reduce to itself via a reduction that does not query on the input string? - Mitoticity: can a complete set be split into two complete sets? Most complete sets have been known to have one or more of these properties. The proposed project aims to address the remaining open questions regarding these properties especially those having major impact in complexity theory if settled. For example, are EXP-complete sets autoreducible for the truth-table reductions? Solving this problem would either separate EXP from PH, or PSPACE from P.

grant.title: Promoting Postbaccalaureate Opportunities for Hispanic Americans (PPOHA) Program
grant.abstract: The University of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC) is a public four-year university that serves more than 17,000 students, over 90 percent of whom are Hispanic coming from the Rio Grande Valley (RGV) region in south Texas. The region is still plagued with a dismaying poverty rate of 36.5 percent in 2008. There is an extremely urgent need in Rio Grande Valley to provide affordable postsecondary education, and produce high-quality graduates with promising employability, in order to bring radical changes to the local economy. To respond to such severe regional situations as well as the national imperative to promote postsecondary education for Hispanic Americans, The University of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College proposes a project to improve its graduate programs in computer science (CS) and math as an effort to expand postbaccalaureate educational opportunities for Hispanic Americans and contribute to the bootstrapping of regional economy. The project aims to (1) improve the retention and graduation rates of Hispanic and low-income graduate students in computer science and math; (2) improve the employability including the ability for Ph.D. study of Hispanic and low-income students upon their graduations; (3) attract more Hispanic and disadvantaged students to enter into Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics fields. Over the life of the grant, the project will integrate proven best practices including: (1) course development consisting of online course development to facilitate convenient access to these courses and improve students’ retention rate, and new course development and course redesign in emerging areas such as bioinformatics, cyber security and distance education in mathematics that will greatly benefit students’ future employment and/or further academic careers; (2) faculty mentored research to engage students in research and keep them motivated and focused on their graduate study to prompt success; (3) high-school outreach and teaching activities to build linkages among computer science or math students towards teaching in high schools and motivate them to pursue a teaching career, as well as to attract more high school teachers/students to pursue computer science and math undergraduate/graduate degrees; (4) summer internship program to enable students to get first-hand industry experience through internships and to be more employable upon graduation; (5) invited speaker series where successful minority students, scholars and industry leaders will be invited as role models to the University of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College to have dialogues with our participating students to inspire them to pursue advanced study in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics; (6) teaming graduate students with undergraduate students in research project as well as in regular academic life through “buddy-mentoring” in order to not only develop the leaderships of graduate students but also engage undergraduate students to strengthen and widen the pipeline in computer science and math through graduate degrees. SUMMIT will establish pipelines, starting from junior years and culminating in the successful admission of the students into Ph.D. programs and subsequent graduation. The SUMMIT pilot project is aimed at scaling into an alliance throughout the state of Texas and extending to the Gulf Coast states where such efforts are acutely needed. SUMMIT will utilize the best practices and will enhance, disseminate, and institutionalize these best practices in the region and at the national level. The SUMMIT program encompasses the following seven major components: (1) An early recruiting and retention plan that places emphasis on early engagement, constant monitoring and encouragement; (2) A two-stage research experience program that includes an advanced research experience workshop at UTA preceded by a preparatory research experience workshop at UTB; (3) Co-advising for students by faculty members at UTA. Participating students will conduct research under co-advising and mentoring by faculty from their home institutions and UTA. This will equip students with necessary research experience to facilitate their transition and admission to the Ph.D. program at a research institution; (4) Student buddy-mentoring. We will match participating students with Ph.D. students at UTA who will serve as buddy-mentors to provide students with informal academic guidance as well as emotional support; (5) Invited Speaker Series. Successful minority students, researchers and scholars in computing will be invited as role models to UTB and UTA during the two respective research workshops to have dialogues with our participating students. They will be the best people to inspire students participating in our project to pursue advanced study and research in computing; (6) A Ph.D. application workshop that includes sessions to help students prepare materials for Ph.D. admission as well as sessions to help students do well in the GRE subject test; (7) Interactive assessment and evaluation. Independent evaluators from social science will be recruited to evaluate the effectiveness of the project.

grant.title: Improving Undergraduate Mathematics Learning through the Innovative Integration of Learning Theories and Touch-Screen Technologies
grant.abstract: The overarching goal of the project is to improve students’ success and the quality of learning collegiate mathematics through introduction of new methodology based upon learning theories accepted by the math education community, and touch-screen technologies (iPad in particular). Touch-screen technologies will be used to create “objects to teach/learn/work with” while learning linear algebra content common for the College Algebra and Linear Algebra courses. Significance of the Project: Incorporation of touch-screen technologies to the college curricula to address recommendations of learning theories is a new approach that, to the best of the proposers’ knowledge, has not been widely utilized so far in teaching college mathematics. Intellectual Merit: The developed methodology and strategy will be an integration of proven learning theories findings (radical constructivism and Stage by Stage Development of Mental Action Theory) with modern touch-screens technology, (particularly I-Pads). The methodology of development of action in a material/materialized form, that involves exercises aimed at the studied properties of the model of action in a materialized form, will be developed. Broader Impact: The project results will have a potential to transform the manner in which undergraduate math education is conducted. It will be scalable to different sizes of student populations and transformable for various areas of mathematics. The developed strategy can be easily incorporated into asynchronous online and/or blended teaching and could impact a large population of students. The developed materials will be as mobile as the I-Pad and will allow students to be engaged in learning, irrespective of their location. A large predominately Hispanic student population will be positively impacted. Project’s Objectives: (1) Improve student disposition toward mathematics; (2) Improve understanding of algebra as a process of modeling and problem solving that produces results; (3) Develop and introduce into teaching of the content that Linear Algebra and College Algebra have in common methodology/strategies that are based on integration of the onstructivism/SSDMA and touch-screen technologies. Create learning materials that support these methodologies/strategies; (4) Develop iPad applications to teach elements of Linear Algebra; (5) Develop mathematics faculty expertise in applying learning theories to teaching collegiate mathematics; (6) Enhance the understanding of how students learn mathematics at the collegiate level in the Touch-Screen Learning Environment in general and iPad in particular: conduct an assessment on how the “quality” of “objects to work with” impact teaching undergraduate mathematics at different levels. Assessment of students’ disposition & understanding dynamics: The team will conduct qualitative assessment to identify aspects of student disposition toward mathematics and understanding of algebra and how those dispositions and understanding change through the use of the iPad learning environment. Evaluation: The project will be evaluated by the external evaluator, who is an expert in the field. Dissemination: The project’s results will be disseminated through a series of workshops, publications and presentations at professional meetings and conferences, and implementation to the teaching practice of other institutions. Collaborative project between Hispanic Serving University and Community College.

grant.title: Distributed Content Based Image Retrieval Systems (D-CBIR)
grant.abstract: We have recently acquired a state-of-the-art data intensive and high performance computing cluster research facility, through the MRI NSF program, which we named Futuro Computing Cluster. The goal of this cluster is to foster interdisciplinary research projects and Computer Science (CS) education programs with the goal of laying a foundation for a strong research and education integration centered on CS at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB). With the recent growth of the amount of multimedia (audio, video, and images) brought about by the proliferation of digital devices, content-based image retrieval (CBIR) systems have become an important task in computer vision and multimedia processing. Coupled with the recent advances in storage media, multiprocessors, and distributed computing, CBIR systems are ripe and well positioned to benefit greatly from distributed and parallel algorithms. The goal of this project is to devise distributed algorithms for well-proven methods in CBIR to reduce the computational complexity of the search engine to be comparable with a text or metadata based one. A second goal is to take full advantage of the available computing resource at hand. In particular, our system is aimed at creating an adaptive system that automatically decides the methodology and optimal set of parameters associated with any of the three important stages in CBIR: features extraction, similarity measures, and decision schemes. The system’s adaptivity should extend to selecting a specific algorithm based on the available computing resources. Existing feature extraction algorithms including color features (such as those based on histograms, moments), texture features (such as those based on Markov random fields, Gabor filters, and wavelets), shape features (such as those based on Fourier descriptors, digital topology) are usually presented for single thread and/or single machine; the same goes for similarity measures (such as the L1 or L2 norms, Min-Max ratio), and many clustering and classification methods (such as K-means, Support Vector Machines, Subspace methods). Our proposed distributed CBIR will be reporting results on different computer architectures including Peer to Peer, Client-Server, and Cluster based. The set of available cooperative nodes can be configured adaptively to provide specific time or space constraints. Depending on the computing resources available, we will investigate the use of both software and hardware supported threads with single and multi-core processors to take full advantage of the available resources.

grant.title: Integrating Synchronous and Asynchronous Components into Graduate Curriculum to Improve Learning Effectiveness and Better Serve Students with Time Constraints
grant.abstract: Hispanics lag behind other major ethnic groups in attaining postsecondary degrees, especially Master’s degrees. Most Hispanic students start their career as soon as they receive their Bachelor's degree. Later they realize that a higher degree, like a Master of Science (MS) in Computer Science (CS), affords more opportunities and better salaries. By that time, it seems too late to return to school because they have already been involved in many responsibilities that discourage them from pursuing any advanced degree. To resolve this dilemma, they may choose between two options. The first option is that they can pursue an online degree from a select online university. However, this option lacks face-to-face interaction with faculty and fellow students which raises a concern regarding the effectiveness of distance learning. Another possibility is to choose a local university that offers both online and face-to-face instruction. Studies show that hybrid (combining online and face-to-face instruction) course offering appears more effective in learning than face-to-face or fully Web-based instruction. Therefore, the second option is obviously more feasible for most students. To better serve the needs of prospective students who have interests in pursuing a higher degree, such as an MS in CS but are not able to attend traditional college due to other commitments, we propose a pilot project to integrate both synchronous and asynchronous components into our graduate curriculum that allows for reduced face-to-face instruction. The goal of the project is to improve the existing graduate program in CS by developing, implementing, and evaluating an innovative hybrid lecturing mode at the University of Texas at Brownsville/Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC), which serves approximately 17,000 students, of which over 90 percent are Hispanic.

grant.abstract: The computing research instrument acquisition described here – of the Futuro computing cluster for interdisciplinary research projects and Computer Science (CS) education programs – seeks to lay the foundation for a strong research and education integration centered on CS at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB), a minority serving institution in the south Texas Rio Grande Valley, a historically underrepresented region with more than 90% Hispanics. The MRI investment will enable promising young investigators to greatly raise the stature of CS research at UTB and in the region, attract new sources of research support, and elevate CS education for Hispanic students to a competitive level. The south Texas valley region has 9 higher education institutions, including research institutions UTB and UT Pan American (UTPA). However, the entire valley does not have a single up-to-date cluster. The current clusters at UTB and UTPA are decommissioned after years of intensive usage. Temporary “cluster” consisting of several PCs is set up to carry on our research projects, which is very limited and non-reliable. Futuro–to be acquired and operated by UTB and shared with UTPA–will serve as a laboratory in which: core research can be conducted at a world-class level; collaborations with on-campus domain sciences provide real-world test applications and expertise to drive significant advances in interdisciplinary research; and significant opportunities are made available to both undergraduates and graduates in CS and related disciplines. Intellectual Merit: Futuro will enable research activities in data mining, pattern discovery, genetic data analysis, experimental astronomical physics, collaborative filtering, theory of computation, high dimensional visualization, and other computational areas. More precisely, it will enable the following activities with transformative goals: (1) terabyte scale data mining and pattern discovery in time series datasets obtained from heterogeneous sensor network; and applying this research to address important data analysis problems in Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO), one of the nation’s most advanced scientific endeavors on the frontiers of physics; (2) Genetic data analysis in complex human diseases to identify totally novel susceptibility factors; this research will enable new understanding of genetic causes of complex diseases such as schizophrenia and thus likely lead to development of new therapeutic strategies for them; (3) studying the dynamical systems and Stellar populations to model the behavior of black hole binaries in globular clusters and galactic nuclei; this research will create models of formation of stellar systems via intensive computation and they can provide important information for interpretation of results from currently operating gravitational wave detectors (such as LIGO and LISA detectors); (4) exploring and creating computing-effective, scalable, robust and intelligent learning algorithms for large recommender systems based on collaborative filtering by incorporating multispectral information; this research will lead to development of next generation recommender systems; (5) visualizing high-dimensional streaming data from heterogeneous sensors; this research will lead to development of new data reduction methodologies, new visualization methodologies that incorporate intelligent computation such as data mining, and thus more advanced visualization systems that has cross-disciplinary utility; and (6) benchmarking and developing algorithms for approximating the NP-hard subgraph isomorphism problem with best possible practical performance; this research will benefit several import application areas such as image recognition and bioinformatics. Broader Impact: The computing services enabled by Futuro will benefit potential users from physics, bioinformatics, computational engineering, and environment engineering at UTB and UTPA. Futuro forms a nucleus for collaboration between computer scientists and researchers from other departments and other institutions, resulting in further funding opportunities. The project’s educational activities will train students in the Rio Grande Valley, in areas of computer science that are expected to have the greatest national impacts in the coming years. More precisely, the CS curriculum will be enriched by lab modules enabled by the cluster facility for providing hands-on experience in parallel programming and scientific computing. As part of the proposed activities, students from computer science, physics and other programs will be involved in exciting and engaging interdisciplinary collaborative research.

grant.title: R&D: Using a Community of Practice Approach to Enhance the Abilities of Computer Education Teachers
grant.abstract: This project aims at developing an effective professional development program for high-school school teachers to address the challenge of how to enhance teachers’ abilities in computer and information sciences (CIS) education in a culturally diverse environment. The participants of our project are predominantly high-school teachers in the Brownsville Independent School District (BISD) in Texas State, who through this project will obtain degrees or credit hours needed to teach computer courses in the Texas Dual Enrollment Program (TDEP) for high-school students. The long term goal of our project is, however, to create and foster a nourishing community of practice (CoP) among peer teachers that promotes productive learning of CIS content knowledge through interactions that develops life-long learning. For the research aspect, we will investigate whether and how such a CoP model integrated with a university-based professional development program in a minority setting will increase the CIS content knowledge and instructional skills of participants that improves their delivery of CIS content in the classroom setting, and develop a culture that increases both instructional and CIS skills. Our project includes the following major components: (1) a graduate program for high-school teachers leading to a master degree in education with a CIS concentration; (2) creation and maintenance of a nourishing community of practice among teachers through regular in-person formal and informal meetings, ad hoc cyber-enabled ways such as online discussion forums, and other possible means; (3) incentive mechanisms including tuition assistance, participant stipends, and articulation agreements with high-school districts to hire only qualified teachers to teach computer courses in the future; (4) involvement of high-school teachers in the curriculum development to create a pipeline between high schools and computing degrees offered by CIS department of UTB; (5) research that investigates the effects of the models developed in this project on CIS learning and teaching of high-school teachers in a minority setting.

grant.title: Rio Grande Valley GAANN Fellowships for Graduate Study in Computer Science at UTB/TSC
grant.abstract: Information technology (IT) is one of the fastest-growing areas of job growth. However, statistics show that IT job growth is outstripping IT degree production for the current decade. In the current stage of economic crisis, if the U.S. economy is to remain globally competitive, we must invest in recruiting, supporting and producing more graduate degrees in the computing disciplines. This investment must occur across all segments of our population, but it is particularly important among those groups who have historically under participated in computing. Hispanic students constitute one such population. The Univ. of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC) is serving over 17000 students, over 90% of which are Hispanic coming from the Rio Grande Valley (RGV) region in south Texas. While RGV is a region of tremendous potential for growth in terms of human capital (the first in the nation) and in terms of contributions this population can make to the state and the nation, such potential cannot be realized without the intellectual and educational resources that have been historically lacking. The region is plagued with a poverty rate of 36.5%, and an estimated median household income of $28,623 in 2008, much lower than the state level $47,548 and national level $50,233. It is impossible for most students in this region to go for graduate level study without financial support. The proposed GAANN program from U.S. Department of Education will provide a critical financial leverage and create exciting opportunities so that prospective graduate students can pursue advanced CS degrees and realize their dream in an academic/industrial career. Through the support of GAANN, the Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) department will award fellowships to graduate students who have excellent academic records and demonstrated financial needs. CIS offers a master level program called Master of Interdisciplinary Studies with concentration in Computer Science (MSIS-CS). MSIS has been in existence since 1992. Computer Science courses within MSIS have been offered since 2002. The proposal plans to award 3 fellowships in each fiscal year of the project. UTB/TSC is committed to match 25% of the amount of grant that Department of Education awards. To ensure that GAANN fellows maintain satisfactory progress toward the completion of their degrees, evaluation will be conducted every semester and fellowships will be renewed annually. The goals of the GAANN project are: 1) to increase the enrollment of graduate students in the MSIS-CS program; 2) to strengthen existing academic pipeline in CIS; 3) to enhance the GAANN fellows’ teaching skills and research capabilities; 4) to enable graduate students to concentrate on course study by providing them full financial support; and 5) to encourage GAANN fellows to pursue Ph.D. degrees in CS at doctorate institutions such as UT San Antonio, UT Dallas and UT Austin. Measurable outcomes are aligned with the goals and will be evaluated during the implementation process of the project to ensure its success.
