An Integrated Framework for High Dimensional Data Reduction, Data Mining, and Data Retrieval
grant.abstract: Technical advances in sensors and data/image acquisition modalities have resulted in a vast amount of raw and complex data in many (sometimes heterogeneous) formats. And despite the parallel increase in the capacity of storage devices and the corresponding decrease in their cost, there is still a tremendous need for novel algorithms to reduce, store, and retrieve the data more efficiently. This need is most critical for applications involving national security functions of the army, the military, and the DoD. Therefore, to support the military needs for these efficient data processing and information extraction algorithms, we propose the creation of an integrated joint framework for combined high dimensional data reduction, image mining and retrieval representation which is based on statistical pattern recognition methods. Our proposed work will strive to connect the three areas in substantive ways, aiming at finding novel and common algorithms among them, and therefore, having the potential to reduce the time and space complexity of the overall systems or devices utilizing them. To overcome the curse of dimensionality, our proposal seeks new and more compact data reduction algorithms by combining the best attributes of Subspace Projections methods, Clustering Methods, and Multi-dimensional Discriminant Analysis. When implemented efficiently, these methods have great effect at reducing the computational and storage requirements when either when storing images or when retrieving them. The same three methodologies will also be used for subsequent image mining and retrieval through clustering functionality, either directly or through some variation. As aside effect, the subspace projections and clustering methods can be efficiently used for visualization through pixel-based and feature-based fusion methods (for example, for multi sensors and imaging modalities). These methods strive to reduce redundant information while complimentary and characteristically intrinsic information from involved modalities is kept and utilized. The proposal will involve our largely Hispanic students and will be closely integrated into the Computer and Information Sciences undergraduate and graduate curriculum through the following: 1) Establishment of Student DoD/CIS Scholarship/Fellowship program; 2) Establishment of the Data Reduction, Data Mining, and Data Retrieval Laboratory (D-RMRL); 3) Close one-on-one mentoring and advising by the PI and Senior Personnel; 4) Required team-projects in a set of identified courses, which include Digital Image Processing, Data Mining, Computer Vision, Databases, and Algorithm Analysis II; 5) Senior Projects and graduate theses for students who will receive fellowships; and 6) Organization of monthly seminars by involved faculty and students.

grant.title: Disjoint NP-pairs and Structural Properties of Complete Sets
grant.abstract: We propose to continue research on disjoint NP-pairs and structural properties of complete sets.Both areas are active and have many interesting and important open problems. We believe that major results in these two areas will shed new lights in computational complexity and bring about a better understanding of fundamental open problems in the area. A disjoint NP-pair is a pair of disjoint, nonempty sets in NP. The study of disjoint NP-pairs is motivated by its connections to secure public-key cryptosystems and to propositional proof complexity. The latter subject is concerned with the complexity of proof systems for propositional logic, which itself is related to the problem of whether NP equals coNP. In a reasonable formulation of public-key cryptosystems, the problem of cracking public-key cryptosystems is equivalent to separating certain disjoint NP-pairs. For this reason, answers to questions about the existence of NP-hard or P-inseparable disjoint NP-pairs informs us about the question of whether secure public-key cryptosystems exist or whether public-key cryptosystems can be NP-hard to crack. Disjoint NP-pairs is also related to propositional proof systems. Razborov associated a canonical (disjoint) NP-pair with every propositional proof system and showed that the canonical NP-pair of an optimal propositional proof system is complete for the class of all disjoint NP-pairs. Recently we much strengthened Razborov’s result by proving that every disjoint NP-pair is equivalent to the canonical NP-pair of some propositional proof system. We also showed that canonical NP-pairs contain certain information about their proof systems. These results display unexpected and interesting connections between disjoint NP-pairs and propositional proof systems. We would like to obtain more results along this line to gain better understandings of both disjoint NP-pairs and propositional proof systems. It is important to study computational structures of complete sets, because they, by reductions of all the sets in the class to the complete sets, represent all of the structure that a class might have. For this reason, the study of structural properties of complete sets gave us a better understanding of the computational power of various complexity classes, and also might lead to proofs of separation results in complexity theory. We will focus on robustness, autoreducibility, and mitoticity in this project. Many complete sets have been known to have one or more of these properties while several questions still remain open. We will continue investigating on this. This project will prompt research and education in theoretical computer science at a Hispanic-serving institution. The PI will develop senior and graduate courses and seminars to teach topics related to this project. The PI’s graduate student will actively engage in the research of this project. We believe that successful completion of the project will greatly foster the interests among students for research in theoretical computer science and for computer science and engineering at large. This project will also contribute to broadening participation of Hispanics in computer science and engineering, who have been historically underrepresented in the area. All results from this project will be disseminated broadly. Our project will be part of the ongoing effort in the computer science community to understand the ultimate nature of computing. The long term goal is to seek answers for fundamental questions on computing such as what can be computed (efficiently) and how. We believe that any major breakthrough regarding these questions will eventually bring radical changes to computer science and information technology, which will in turn benefit human society in this age of information.

grant.title: Experimental Analysis of Algorithms for NP-hard Optimization Problems
grant.abstract: Efficient algorithms are among the core techniques in the advancement of many areas of computer science such as computer networking, database or emerging areas including bioinformatics or information retrieval. The past decade has seen rising interest in experimental analysis of algorithms among the computer science community; it emphasizes studying algorithms’ performance through experimental runs that mimic “typical” and common real situations. This project will follow the current research trend and focus on experimental analysis of algorithms for several NP-hard optimization problems (Satisfiability, Bin Packing and Traveling Salesman). NP-hard optimization problems are important in theoretical and applied computer science. However, the best algorithms known for these problems are either approximation algorithms or algorithms with exponential time complexity. We will try to understand and implement these algorithms, carry out experimental analysis, and investigate what implementation techniques are needed to achieve their theoretical performance. Based on the results of our experimental analysis, we will also seek improvements of the algorithms, both at theoretical and implementation levels. Successful completion of the project will give us a deeper understanding of the best theoretical algorithms to-date for NP-hard optimization problems, their practical efficiency and ways of improving them. Another component of our project includes the implementations of the aforementioned algorithms that can be used in real applications and/or in competitions for those algorithms. Besides technical goals, our project aims to strengthen research in theoretical computer science within the Department of CS/CIS at UTB. This is critical for building a full-fledged computer science research and education program within a minority-serving institution.

The ISP proposed will identify the needs of participating students for basic learning skills and at the same time incorporate contextualized learning, with focus on helping students to grasp subject matter in sciences, into the classroom. Believing that college learning is an interactive process, the participating faculty will also introduce peer cooperative learning as an integral part of classroom activity, such as peer reviewing and group brainstorming. In addition, the faculty will hold conferences with students on a regular basis to diagnose patterns of errors and provide help tailored to each student’s special needs.

grant.title: Beowulf Based Curriculum Enrichment Integrated Laboratory (B-CEIL)
grant.abstract: A Beowulf cluster is a low-cost supercomputer based on inexpensive computer nodes networked together. It provides a low-cost parallel processing environment that can be used to enrich curricula in computer science and related fields at the associate's and bachelor's levels. This project is developing a Beowulf-Based Curriculum Enrichment Integrated Laboratory (B-CEIL) for enhancing important concepts and principles in key courses of several degree programs: B.S. in computer science, Associate of Applied Science (A.A.S.) in computer information systems, and Bachelor of Applied Technology (B.A.T.). The central component of the lab is a 24-node Beowulf cluster, built from an existing inventory of 24 Pentium computers and three Alpha workstations, with the addition of complementary equipment to simulate a Public Switched Network (PSN). Two levels of student lab projects are being developed in the B-CEIL environment. The first level covers topics such as computer interfacing, networking, clustering, task scheduling and optimization, and benchmarking. The second level focuses on enhancing students' understanding of real-world PSN-based networking and computationally intensive fields such as artificial neural networks, image compression, image analysis, numerical analysis, and distributed databases. The student lab projects are applicable to a number of courses in the university's B.S., A.A.S., and B.A.T. programs, including Networking, Systems Programming and Concurrent Processes, Computer Organization, Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, Principles of Programming Languages, Numerical Methods, Image Processing, and PC Hardware.

grant.title: Advancing Manufacturing Capabilities - Exploring the application of Drones for Material Handling and Quality Control in Manufacturing Industries
grant.abstract: The evolution of industrial systems toward Industry 4.0 depends on the interconnectivity of products and processes throughout the whole manufacturing life cycle. Industry 4.0; characterized by emerging technologies of advanced data analytics, robotics, and automation; has a huge potential to reshape the manufacturing industry in several domains within the next 5 to 10 years. This shift in manufacturing production systems is influencing the demand for the use and integration of autonomous systems in manufacturing production. Towards addressing this need, the primary goal of this project is to explore the application of unmanned aerial vehicles, commonly known as drones, in manufacturing to automate Quality Control processes and Material Handling tasks in highly complex environments such as factories, storage facilities, and warehouses. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (A) Engaging with subject matter experts and professionals from manufacturing industries to explore and identify opportunities and challenges for integrating drones in manufacturing, (B) Develop an interactive drone-based online quality control system for product and process inspection to be deployed and tested using applied use cases in manufacturing industries, and (C) To explore the application and logistics of drone-drone co-operative manipulation (DDCM) and human-drone co-operative manipulation (HDCM) in manufacturing industries through computational modeling, simulations, and prototypes. This project successfully executed has the potential to substantially advance the state-of-the-art quality control processes and logistics in future manufacturing through a novelty harvesting of the potential of robotic-drone platforms.

This project supported by its design addresses the significant factors, which influence the retention of Hispanic students in STEM based curricula. The hybrid approach in identifying activities that overlap student curricula and the proposed student support system will improve student learning experience along with introducing them to emerging technology trends. This project will ultimately establish a platform for increasing the retention of students in STEM.

grant.title: R-LAB(Robotics Lab in a Phone) - Introducing underrepresented students to STEM career pathways through Robotics in an Informal Setting
grant.abstract: This pilots and feasibility studies AISL project aims to provide a quality STEM learning experience by providing opportunities to middle school and high school students to get exposed to the basics of engineering (i.e., in electronics, robotics, programming, and applied mathematics) at the intersection of Mobile-based learning and Robotics. The primary goal of this project is to develop an effective mechanism for underrepresented and low-income middle school and high school students to stimulate their participation and increase their awareness in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). At the core of this project, we propose to design and develop a pilot robotic kit that consists of a 3D-printed robotic arm manipulator with an integrated mobile-based application (R-LAB) to guide students to first build and later program the robotic arm manipulator. This robotic kit is aimed to provide students with an informal learning experience with minimal supervision. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include (1) Designing and developing pilot robotic kits to be distributed among 75 middle and high school students from the Brownsville Independent School District (BISD). Each kit will be composed of a 3D printable robotic arm manipulator and a mobile-based smartphone application that will guide students in building and programming the robotic arm; (2) Organizing virtual and in-person family café sessions where STEM industry and academic speakers will be invited to interact with students and their parents in order to promote STEM professions; and (3) Conducting guided virtual and in-person industry tours to local industries in the Rio Grande Valley to provide students with a real-life approach to what engineering is. Guided by an integrated STEM learning framework tailored for informal learning, this project aims to demystify the field of engineering and encourage students to reevaluate career choices and pursue a STEM profession. In addition, by using the proposed R-LAB smart-phone application, students will have opportunities to explore engineering and coding in an informal context.

Direct Torque Control of Electric Current Phase and Frequency in the Permanent-Magnet Synchronous Generator
presentation.event: International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and Computers and Information in Engineering Conference
presentation.abstract: The control design, formal stability analysis, and simulation results of a direct-torque controller applied to the permanent magnet synchronous generator (PMSG) is presented here. The controlled variables are the PMSG’s phase, amplitude, and frequency of the alternating current (AC) signal. For control design purposes and computer simulation, the PMSG is modeled in the frame of reference. On the other hand, the control algorithm is designed via backstepping technique and Lyapunov asymptotic stability is demonstrated for tracking error of the mechanical velocity and the electrical current. Uniform asymptotic stability is proved in a twofold procedure. First, it is shown that both mechanical and electrical subsystems of the PMSG are input to state stable with respect to conveniently selected inputs. Second, uniform asymptotic stability of the interconnected mechanical and electrical subsystems is shown via Lyapunov’s stability direct method. Finally, the performance of the closed-loop system, composed of the PMSG model and the control algorithm, is tested via numerical simulations, which show that the three-phase electric currents in the PMSG and the rotor’s mechanical velocity track the imposed reference signals. Keywords: Wind energy systems, permanent magnet synchronous generator, backstepping control, input to state stability, Lyapunov stability.

presentation.title: THE EFFECT OF THE BALANCE BOARD MASS ON THE STABILITY, EQUILIBRIUM, AND ROBUSTNESS OF THE HUMAN-BALANCE BOARD SYSTEM
presentation.event: International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and Computers and Information in Engineering Conference
presentation.abstract: People with neuromuscular deficits may show balance issues that put them in high risk of fall. To reduce the risk, balance-board (BB)-based rehabilitation intervention has been widely used. However, despite the extensive use of BB-based interventions, the mechanisms responsible for rehabilitation remain unclear. To better understand these mechanisms; several studies have used a system dynamics approach to investigate the effect of neuromuscular deficits (visual, vestibular, proprio-ceptive) and sensorimotor latencies on the stability and dynamical behavior of the human-BB system. Though, to the best knowledge of the authors, the effect of the BB mass on the stability and dynamics of the human-BB system has never been investigated. In the present study, bifurcation analyses, root finding techniques, and computational simulations are used to investigate the effect of the BB mass and BB time-delay on the stability, equilibrium, and robustness of the human-BB upright posture (UP) for cases where either proprioceptive or visual and vestibular deficits are considered in simulation. The results show that the BB mass and time-delay play a critical role on the UP stability, leaning postures, and robustness of the human-BB system. In fact, increasing BB mass reduces the range of neuromuscular gains that stabilize the system and shrinks the basin of attraction of the UP, which is related to the human-BB system’s robustness to posture disturbances. This effect is more evident in the case where visual and vestibular deficits are considered in simulation. This relationship may have implications on the design and development of BBs with tunable mass and tunable time-delay. presentation.title: Weak Mitoticity of Bounded Conjunctive and Disjunctive Autoreducible Sets
presentation.event: 15th Annual International Computing and Combinatorics Conference
presentation.abstract: Glaßer et al. (SIAMJCOMP 2008 and TCS 2009 (The two papers have slightly different sets of authors)) proved existence of two sparse sets A and B in EXP, where A is 3-tt (truth-table) polynomial-time autoreducible but not weakly polynomial-time Turing mitotic and B is polynomial-time 2-tt autoreducible but not weakly polynomial-time 2-tt mitotic. We unify strengthen both of those results by showing that there is a sparse set in EXP that is polynomial-time 2-tt autoreducible but not even weakly polynomial-time Turing mitotic. All these results indicate that polynomial-time autoreducibilities in general do not imply polynomial-time mitoticity at all with the only exceptions of the many-one and 1-tt reductions. On the other hand, however, we proved that every autoreducible set for the polynomial-time bounded disjunctive or conjunctive tt reductions is weakly mitotic for the polynomial-time tt reduction that makes logarithmically many queries only. This shows that autoreducible sets for reductions making more than one query could still be mitotic in some way if they possess certain special properties.

presentation.title: Mining Dependent Patterns
presentation.abstract: Association Rule (AR) mining has been studied intensively for the past two decades. Essentially, AR models the conditional probabilities of itemsets. However, AR mining generates an overwhelming number of rules which limits its capability in mining real nuggets. We re-examined the problem and propose to start mining on dependent relationships instead of conditional relationships. In contrast to AR mining, dependence mining has received much less attention in the literature. Here a new model, Dependent Pattern (DP) mining is presented. DP has a solid base in classical statistics and at the same time is suitable for large scale computation with the property of downward closure. We validate the model from different perspectives using a variety of datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that DP has remarkable advantages over AR mining and other related methods. This work serves as a proof of concept. Future work will focus on the theoretical analysis of DP’s scalability.
